content: Currently, inhaled corticosteroids are the primary treatment for managing chronic asthma in children. While they are highly effective in controlling asthma symptoms, the long-term side effects of inhaled corticosteroids in children remain uncertain and are not well-documented. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of inhaled nedocromil sodium compared to a placebo in treating chronic asthma in children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted, including the Cochrane Airway Group trials register, review articles, reference lists, and abstracts from major respiratory society meetings. The drug manufacturer and primary study authors were also contacted for additional information. The most recent search was completed in November 2009. The review included randomized, placebo-controlled trials that compared nedocromil sodium to placebo in children aged 0 to 18 years with chronic asthma. Both authors independently assessed the quality of the trials and extracted relevant data. Additional information was sought directly from the study authors when necessary. A total of 15 trials were included in the analysis, comprising 12 parallel-group studies and 3 crossover trials, with a total of 1,422 children (837 males and 585 females). The studies were generally of good methodological quality. Two large, long-term studies evaluated the use of nedocromil sodium over six months and four to six years, but the results regarding symptom-free days were inconsistent. In contrast, short-term studies lasting between 4 and 12 weeks demonstrated that nedocromil sodium led to improvements in several efficacy measures compared to placebo. These measures included forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), forced vital capacity (FVC), FEV1 as a percentage of predicted values (FEV1% predicted), PC20 FEV1 (a measure of airway hyperresponsiveness), evening peak expiratory flow (PEF), and symptom scores. Parental assessments of efficacy also favored nedocromil, with an odds ratio of 0.5 (95% confidence interval 0.3 to 0.8). Nedocromil sodium was found to have a favorable safety profile, with the only significant side effect being an unpleasant taste. There was limited evidence to suggest a clear dose-response relationship, and only a small number of studies included children with severe asthma. The authors concluded that while a limited number of small studies have shown that nedocromil sodium can improve lung function and some symptom measures, the evidence regarding the primary outcomes of the review was conflicting. The two long-term studies did not consistently demonstrate benefits in lung function, whereas several short-term studies showed positive effects. The variability in results may be due to differences in baseline asthma severity, with children who had milder asthma experiencing less benefit. Additionally, publication bias may have contributed to the discrepancies. Nedocromil sodium has a very good safety profile, with no significant short-term or long-term adverse effects. Although it may offer advantages over inhaled corticosteroids in terms of side effects, further direct comparisons between nedocromil sodium and inhaled corticosteroids are needed to determine whether they provide similar levels of asthma control, particularly in children with mild asthma. At present, the role of nedocromil sodium in the broader context of asthma treatment in children remains unclear.
